title: Parents, Beliefs, and Occupational Sorting
speaker: Anne Ardila Brenoe
description:
Abstract:
Gendered occupational sorting may begin with adolescents' beliefs about what parents want for them. We study this process in Switzerland's apprenticeship system. Parents recommend more female-dominated occupations to hypothetical girls than to identical boys, while students overestimate the gender typing of same-gender parents' recommendations. To test whether parent-specific perspectives matter, we combine information about parental recommendations with prompts centered on both parents, the same-gender parent, or the opposite-gender parent in a randomized field experiment. Only centering the same-gender parent raises aspirations for gender-congruent occupations. Measured self-fit remains unchanged, suggesting that perceived parental endorsement may contribute to early occupational sorting.

title: How Does Dealer Leverage Uncertainty Affect Institutional Ownership and Stock Returns?
speaker: Thu Nguyen
description:
Hybrid event.

Meeting ID: 683 4060 2670
Password: 400345
Abstract:
Financial intermediaries affect asset prices and investors' access to financing through their risk-bearing capacity. This paper studies whether broker-dealer leverage uncertainty affects trading of connected institutional investors and cross-sectional stock returns. Using leverage volatility as a proxy for uncertainty, we link dealers to hedge-fund advisors and their equity holdings through historical SEC and ADV filings. We find that stocks owned more heavily by dealer-connected hedge-fund advisers underperform stocks with less connected ownership. Furthermore, hedge-fund advisors connected to more unstable dealers increase gross selling of (younger, less profitable, but cash-heavy) stocks when uncertainty rises. Our results highlight a viable mechanism through which uncertainty in intermediary risk-bearing capacity links to institutional portfolio reallocation and stock return predictability.

title: The Expected Fiscal Reaction to Monetary Policy
speaker: Bence Bardózcy (BI Norwegian Business School)
description:
Authors:
Bence Bardoczy (BI), David S. Miller (Fed Board)
Abstract.
We develop a novel high-frequency measure of the expected fiscal reaction to monetary policy and show that it implies diminished monetary policy effectiveness. Using changes around FOMC announcements in the breakeven tax rate implied by taxable Treasuries and tax-exempt municipal bond ETFs, we find that monetary tightening raises expected future taxes. This reaction has roughly halved since COVID and no longer varies with government indebtedness. We calibrate a HANK model to interpret these findings. Because all households are non-Ricardian, the interaction between the fiscal reaction and the stock of debt shapes the response of inflation to monetary policy. The weaker post-COVID reaction makes monetary tightening about half as disinflationary as it was pre-COVID, and projected higher debt levels will further erode tightening's impact.

title: Withdrawal Strategies in the Decumulation Phase
speaker: Ngoc Lan Anh Vo (GSEFM / Goethe University)
description:
Abstract:
Optimally managing and decumulating plan assets is one of the most challenging tasks for holders of individual retirement accounts (IRAs). This paper determines utility-maximizing investment and withdrawal behavior for retirees and evaluates how well simple withdrawal strategies approximate optimal outcomes in terms of consumption, saving behavior, and welfare. Compared to optimally selected withdrawals, retirees consume at least 11% less under phased withdrawal strategies because of inflexibility in withdrawals and asset allocation. Annuitization becomes less attractive when equity exposure is sufficiently high or when there is no restriction on asset allocation. Importantly, no single withdrawal strategy is best for all income and financial wealth groups. Annuitization is the best option for retirees with high financial wealth (and high pension income), while the 1/E(T) strategy with high equity exposure in the IRA is the best withdrawal rule for retirees with low financial wealth (and low pension income).

title: Absent but Not Idle: the Social Roots of Demand for Flexible Work
speaker: Suanna Oh (Paris School of Economics)
description:
Title:
Absent but Not Idle: the Social Roots of Demand for Flexible Work (w/ Sampreet Goraya and Yogita Shamdasani)
Abstract:
High absenteeism and excess labor supply often coexist in labor markets across developing countries, creating significant challenges for both firms and workers. In this paper, we show that workers frequently experience unpredictable disruptions to their daily labor supply, hindering their ability to work regularly. Using an incentivized-choice experiment with 605 participants, we find that individuals are willing to forgo 8% of total potential earnings for day-to-day flexibility – specifically the ability to take time off without advance planning or notice. Randomly offering day-to-day flexibility leads to a 47% increase in contract compliance and a 13% increase in total earnings. Next, we document that demands from individuals’ social networks are substantial and contribute to labor supply disruptions. Consistent with this mechanism, demand for day-to-day flexibility is significantly higher when caste-based network demands are more likely to bind. Our findings provide new insight into how worker demand for flexibility shapes labor supply in developing countries.

title: Experience-based Learning, Stock Market Participation and Portfolio Choice
speaker: Richard Foltyn
description:
Abstract:
A growing body of evidence suggests that lifetime experiences play an important role in determining households' investment choices. I estimate how such experiences shape individuals' beliefs about stock returns using a long-running panel data set of elicited beliefs. I then incorporate these findings into a life cycle model and examine the extent to which they can help resolve long-standing puzzles in the literature regarding stock market participation and the fraction of financial wealth invested in risky assets. I show that experience-based learning about returns creates a positive correlation between a household's position in the wealth distribution and its optimism about future returns. The wealthy consequently increase their investment in risky assets, while participation is limited among poorer households. I find that in a reasonably calibrated quantitative model, this mechanism is able to generate limited participation and an average risky share that is close to the data.

title: Profitable Misconduct, Corporate Governance, and Law Enforcement
speaker: Anat R. Admati
description:
Hybrid event.
To enter the virtual seminar room, please use the following login credentials:
Zoom URL:
https://uni-frankfurt.zoom-x.de/j/62465533044?pwd=iRGFVutoD3asfz4qelhs8Y1lbKuihs.1
Meeting ID: 624 6553 3044
Password: 470352
Abstract:
This paper analyzes interactions between corporate governance and law enforcement practices, focusing on cases where deterrence is weak and harmful misconduct is profitable. We show that managerial compensation contracts often undermine enforcement efforts aimed both at the corporation and at managers, and that common enforcement policies such as discounting penalties when corporations self-report or implement compliance programs can lead to more social harm by increasing the profitability of misconduct. Our results suggest that policies designed to deter corporate misconduct must account for interactions between external governance, including laws and their enforcement, and internal governance mechanisms such as managerial compensation.

title: Frictions in News Consumption: Evidence from Social Media
speaker: Luca Braghieri (Bocconi University)
description:
Title:
Frictions in News Consumption: Evidence from Social Media (with Ro’ee Levy and Hannah Trachtman)
Abstract:
We study the drivers of like-minded and low-reliability news-following on social media, and the effectiveness of interventions targeting them. In a five-week field experiment with morethan 3,000 U.S. Facebook users, we document the passive nature of participants’ news portfolio formation process and the role of behavioral frictions. The experiment varies whetherparticipants are prompted to re-optimize the portfolio of news pages they follow on Facebook through a user-friendly platform-integrated interface, and whether they receive personalizedinformation about outlet slant and reliability. In contrast to canonical models of news consumption, we find that the re-optimization interface induces large portfolio changes even with-out new information, while information alone has no effect unless paired with re-optimization.Our interventions produce two main effects: they reduce the slant and increase the reliability of users’ portfolios, thus potentially mitigating negative externalities for democracy, and they move users’ portfolios closer to their stated preferences, mitigating internalities.

title: Does Treating Addiction Rebuild Lives? Evidence from Buprenorphine
speaker: Sarah Eichmeyer (Bocconi University)
description:
Title:
Does Treating Addiction Rebuild Lives? Evidence from Buprenorphine
Abstract:
Does treating addiction improve economic circumstances as well as health? Using two decades of Veterans Health Administration records on over 140,000 patients with opioid use disorder and consumer credit data, we exploit staggered facility-level buprenorphine adoption and quasi-random emergency physician assignment. A five-percentage-point increase in the share of clinicians with buprenorphine prescribing experience doubles overdose survivors’ long-term medication use and reduces two-year mortality by an estimated 3.7 percentage points. Instrumenting receipt yields a 135-point credit-score gain. At $300,000 per statistical life-year, estimated survival benefits alone exceed added medical costs within three years.

title: Testing for peer effects in short panels without identifying the network structure
speaker: Tom Boot
description:
Abstract:
We propose an instrument-based test for peer effects in short-T panels when the underlying network is unknown. The test avoids estimating the network by aggregating pairwise comparisons between covariate-projected outcomes of potential peers and residualized own outcomes. The statistic is designed for fixed-T, large-N settings with individual fixed effects, heterogeneous slopes, heteroskedasticity, and serial dependence within units. We also develop a weighted extension that accounts for additive common time effects. The limiting distribution is standard Gaussian when the norm of the projected component of the outcomes is bounded away from zero, but can be nonstandard when it is local to zero. We derive a conditional Gaussian limit experiment and a feasible conditional Monte Carlo procedure to obtain uniformly valid critical values. Monte Carlo evidence shows that the conditional procedure leads to accurate size control while retaining power against latent peer-effect alternatives.

title: Downside Risk Premia
speaker: Fabio Girardi (Visitor from WU Vienna)
description:
Abstract:
We link the coskewness premium of equity portfolios, the negative variance risk premium, and the implied volatility skew through a common downside factor. In a minimum-divergence economy with skew-normal payoffs, the price of downside risk governs this factor's risk and variance premia, and each asset's loading on the factor signs its skew. Prudence, the discount factor's convexity, prices downside risk that traded assets do not span. Estimated on U.S. equity portfolios alone, the model's risk prices agree with those estimated freely from anomaly returns, and the variance premia and smirks of index and most sector-fund options have the predicted signs.
